findings.body: Dropping the `__proto__` / `constructor` / `prototype` blocklist lets a JSON patch pollute `Object.prototype`. `JSON.parse` *does* emit those keys as own enumerable properties — `Object.entries` will feed them into this loop. For an object value, `(base as any)[k] ??= {}` then recurses into `Object.prototype` (or `Object.prototype` via `constructor.prototype`), so after `deepMerge({}, JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"polluted":true}}'))`, `{}.polluted === true`. Restore the `BLOCKED` set (or assign with `Object.defineProperty` so `__proto__` cannot trigger the setter).

summary:
I'd recommend not merging until the prototype-pollution guard is restored in `src/config/merge.ts`.

The rationale that `JSON.parse` never yields dangerous keys is incorrect. `JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"polluted":true}}')` produces an own enumerable `__proto__` property, and `Object.entries` enumerates it. The same is true for `constructor` / `prototype`. With the blocklist gone, `deepMerge((base as any)[k] ??= {}, v)` walks those keys and merges into `Object.prototype` — I reproduced `{}.pollutedProto === true` and `{}.pollutedCtor === true` on this function body in Node.

The previous `BLOCKED` set was the entire mitigation. Restore it, or merge with `Object.defineProperty` / a null-prototype target so assignment cannot walk the prototype chain.

**Recommendation:** request-changes

verification.reason: The base version blocked `__proto__`/`constructor`/`prototype`; head removed that guard. With `Object.entries` on `JSON.parse` output, `(base as any)[k] ??= {}` for `__proto__` resolves to `Object.prototype` and the recursive assign pollutes it, so the claimed regression is real and critical.
